entries.s: "When I first had a look at the 512b/1k Tiny SID compo, I thought it'd be a great way to get back into doing some assembly language on the C=64 (which I haven't done for a long time). I spent a fair amount of time thinking of the best way to reduce the size and decided that one of the best ways would be to really challenge myself and to squeeze some music out of 128 bytes just for fun. I really wanted to feature the nature of the C=64, so I thought about several ways to best store the note and instrument data. After a few sketches, I found that I seemed to be wasting a lot of space trying to store both the note and duration data, so I decided that the best way would be to derive the notes and durations directly from the C=64 memory and just index into a basic blues scale and generate some music. It took a bit of playing around with techniques, but I found that utilizing individual bits to step up or down within the scale generated the most musical results. Somewhat of a 1-bit DPCM technique except for successive music notes in a scale instead of successive samples. So, the code basically cycles through the bits which are displayed in the screen memory and uses them to generate the notes. The note duration is set by combining the jiffy clock and the cursor countdown to give some flex to the tempo. I found that staying in one note sequence was boring, so I made it step through two blues scales. I tried to squeeze out more space by removing the low byte of the frequency but found that it either made the music too out of tune or too high in pitch. I also attempted to add a second voice, but ran out of space. I really liked the idea of adding something to watch while it's playing, so the colours change as it is reading through the bytes of screen memory. Rolling the bits of screen memory had the additional benefit that the bytes would return to their original form after passing over them eight times when the sequence repeats. The speech says: "Earth, a desolate land witness of an epic battle. Alone against death, your Varkan fighter is braving the nightmare. The legend is in your hands.". the voice belongs to Andrea Pompili.

Andrea Carboni, the programmer of the game, said in an interview: "I never met Michael Tschoegl, who was contacted by Genias directly. The first music disk was completely broken when it arrived, so I recovered all that I could (almost) hear and composed the full tunes from the beginning. When I got the second disk, I realised that the tunes I modified, were not composed for the game parts I used them in. Moreover, they told me that my compositions were a lot better than his!!! Only the final track, the one that plays during the end titles (tune #6), remained untouched. Furthermore, I didn't write about this on the title screen, since actually the basic sound was created by Michael anyway." (info comes from an interview at www.retrogaming.it) Almost the same as /GAMES/M-R/Neverending_Story_II.sid, Tune #2. Necronom Intro [from the Amiga game] Michael Tschögl Composed by Andrea Pompili. He said in an interview: "The groove in the ingame tune was composed by me, and it's based upon a short piece I used to play during the introduction of my band." The game chooses one of three tunes to play at random for the in-game music, based on the value of the C64's timer, and chooses again at the end of play to make the in-game soundtrack. Subtune #1 in this rip replicates this so will play a random choice of the tunes. Subtunes #2 to #4 have been added to play each tune individually. Plays tune #2, #3 and #4 in random order. Blue Is The Colour Daniel Boone & Rod McQueen Performed by Chelsea FC for their 1972 League Cup final single, and an anthem played at the club since then. Nice One Cyril Harold Spiro & Helen Clarke (The Cockerel Chorus) Made for Tottenham Hotspur FC for their 1973 League Cup final single, and sung on the terrces by fans since then. I'm Forever Blowing Bubbles John Kelette Adopted by West Ham United FC during the 1940s as a popular football chant, and has been used by their fans since then. The club also re-recorded the song for their 1975 FA Cup final single.

This is a remix of /MUSICIANS/M/Mueller_Markus/Coco_Intro.sid In a demo by Edwin van Santen, which he released about two years after Coco Intro was made popular in the Papillion's crack intro, he claims that he in fact composed the music. This demo contained a new version of the tune (this SID). He explains how he had made the music two years earlier on some composer like Soundmonitor or something similar. While at a copyparty, someone supposedly stole his music disk which had the tune on it. This was his only copy of the tune. About two months later, the tune appeared on a Papillions' intro and no credit was given to van Santen. See /MUSICIANS/M/Mueller_Markus/Coco_Intro.sid for more details. Lambada Kaoma "I can tell you that the Lambada tune, used in our demo's/openings are from me. At that time I hadn't any player and I didn't want to spend too much time in making one. I ripped the 20CC player by analyzing the code in assembler. Then I programmed the codeblocks myself to get the Lambada tune right. I laughed when 20CC found out that their player was used and Falco Paul or Edwin van Santen hadn't made that tune earlier!!! They accused me of ripping routines etc. etc. Well.. they were right, I never claimed that it was my player but I merged my Lambada tune blocks via assembler into their old music blocks (I overwrote it). The funniest thing was that the Lambada tune from me was very populair at that time. When 20CC heard it they made their own Lambada tune, hehehehe..." (Patrick Peters)

"I was thrown into the deep end with this. I had three weeks to produce the music and sound effects for the C64, Spectrum, and Amstrad versions, which included time to write a music driver for the C64. It was a good learning experience but I wish I had more time to work on the tunes as most of my efforts went into writing the software. I remember listening to the music form The Last Ninja and Wizball at that time, trying to figure out how they created the sounds so I could write my music driver. Martin Galway later told me how he created the high pitched wooden block 'pop' sound, which was achieved by running the driver at 240Hz." (GB) Gary Biasillo's own comments are denoted (GB).

"I programmed and produced the music and sound effects for this game which was the first for the company I set up with my friend Mike Williams called Imperial Software. I had learned a lot of techniques from the talented guys at Ocean and put them to work in this game. 32 sprite multiplexing, near full-screen colour scrolling, and sampled sounds." "I wrote most of Thunder Force together with my highschool friend Peter Uhd Jespsen. The game was originally written for the Danish company called Keleline. Peter was a big fan of Depeche Mode and had most of their records. Therefore we wanted to get some tunes from DM in the game. Keleline wrote to DM and first got a yes, but then the group decided no. At least that was the story we were told, but I think, that the director of the company cheated us. Somewhere out there is a small demo, which have the five tunes in it." Mystified [from the Amiga MOD module] Jogeir Liljedahl Prior to public release, GRG believed this tune was originally done on the Amiga by Liljedahl. According to GRG, when fellow countryman Geir Tjelta heard the SID, Tjelta informed GRG that he thought the original was actually done by Bug (Stein Erik Giske) rather than Liljedahl. Tjelta also informed GRG that Bug passed away in 1992 thus giving GRG inspiration to rename the tune before releasing publicly. Unfortunately Tjelta's credit information was incorrect, however Tjelta does not recall giving GRG incorrect credits perhaps suggesting there was a miscommunication between the two. Another theory is that there may have been confusion between Jogeir's "Mystified" and one of Bug's tunes named "Slider" where the first few notes are similar but indeed the two tunes are very different. Reflecting back, Jogeir Liljedahl, a friend and group member of the late Bug, adds the following: "When it comes to Mystified, it's 100% my original tune. I haven't even thought about the similarities to Bug's Slider tune, but the 5-6 first notes of the song are similar to Mystified. But it's a completely different song of course. Either me or Bug noticed that back then, and Bug was a huge fan of Mystified, since he was among the first to hear the song (along with Olav Rasmus Vorren aka Shorty)." "'Last Flight' is the song about a person which is taking drugs. It is a sad story for both the family to the user, and the user itself, which later in the song dies, it's the user's last flight. The family which stands back with their dead son or daughter is so unhappy and sad that they don't know anything anymore. They're feeling a huge emptyness inside, they only wish their child back again, staying alive. But that will never happen... The last few minutes when the child was alive, it dreamed about a sky of marvelous and wonderful things flying all around. The longer it lasted the longer away this person was to all real things we know here on earth. This child, so young, has left the world. Not alive anymore. Doesn't exist, only the body left for the family to bury and their memories to keep. Why do some want to legalize it?" (KN) Sadly, Kjell Nordbø passed away in June 2005. Dance of the Yao People Liu Tieshan and Mao Yüan Composed in 1950, "Dance of the Yao People" combined folk melodies and rhythms of the Yao people from the Yunan province, southwestern China. Information comes from the liner notes for "Phases of the Moon", a 1981 compact disk published by CBS Records. "Fred Milgrom (founder of MH) gave me heaps of latitude, for which I can only be grateful. I actually studied Chinese and Japanese recordings and instruments for some of these pieces, absurdly serious as that may sound." "The inspiration for the tune came from the arcade game 'Zero Wing', especially that noisy rhythm pattern! The song is very short, and features a very fast solo at the end which is one of my most favorite things in the whole collection. In the last part there's a little joke: the tune goes 'lo-fi' (only three rectangular waveforms are used), and some sound effects play along; this should give the idea of someone actually playing a game! If you listen carefully, you can figure out what is happening: the player shoots some alien robots, gets some power-ups and eventually gets hit! I had a lot of fun composing this part, as I had to design the sound effects too!" (GC) Gaetano Chiummo's own comments are denoted (GC).

"History of Headaches is another piece I like very much. This tune was composed for a Tape Loader Compo, and I wanted it to sound like Galway's Ocean Loaders tunes, without using any drums and trying to have the bass playing the rhythmical part. I also didn't want to 'multiplex' too much, and leave each note play without being stopped abruptly by the next one. There's also an 'echo' effect on the lead instrument, which gives more depth to the sound." (GC) Gaetano Chiummo's own comments are denoted (GC).

"I composed the main harmony on guitar, and then finished the tune and arranged it on Psycle, trying to figure out how I could use the three SIDs at their best. The most obvious thing to do was to dedicate one SID to the chords (this was a bit limiting, as I could only use three notes chords), another SID to the lead instrument and the bass, and another one to the drums. As for the lead instrument, I could use two tracks: one for the main instrument, and the other one for a counter melody or for some special effects, such as the 'sync'. As for the drums, the snare and the hi-hat used two voices both, while the bass drum only played on one track: this made the arrangement a bit difficult, as I didn't want to make any instrument sound 'stopped'." (GC) Gaetano Chiummo's own comments are denoted (GC).

"[...] But now let me tell something about this music. It was composed and tracked within hours on january, 23rd. This is a kind of jazz tune, it's not my style ya know, but I felt like doing a tune like this because lots a people like it. Therefore I added sum of my music style to the tune, that's why it sounds a bit techno like.. Try to enjoy this tune with a stereo, you'll like it I guess.. By the way remember that all C128 computers have a different filter set on their SID chips,so the music sounds a bit different than on normal C64 computers, you'll hear the difference on the bass, the filters doesn't open theirselves so much on C128! "I quite like composing to a strict brief and this was one of those projects where I felt the oriental feel was essential. It was the first time I went and talked in detail to the story-boarders and then included some sound fx in the music track; the ship creaking, the ship's bell, etc. This kind of sound mix is now absolutely commonplace in modern games. In fact, what goes into a soundtrack nowadays, we could only dream about back in the 80's. But, this was an early, basic attempt to get some atmosphere into the game." With the aid of the software house CRL and distributor Nu Wave, Mike Oldfield released this as an interactive C64 version of the album in 1986 accompanied by some simple 2D visual effects. The interactivity offered by the album/program was limited to controlling the speed and quantity of the visual effects, tuning the sound's volume and filtering, and skipping to any part of the album. It can be considered the first example of a commercial interactive computer demo or "musicdisk". Airwolf Theme [from the TV series] Sylvester Levay "When I was interviewed by Brian Wilcox at Elite for a job they sent me home with a little task to prove that I had some computer and progamming skills. The task was to make the Oric Atmos computer I had at home play the theme tune to Airwolf. Over the weekend I managed to get the tune playing using a very simple assembler that I had written in basic. As a result I got the job at Elite and the first thing they had me doing was programming the Airwolf tune on the C64 as they were doing a game based on the TV show. After this I found myself doing music all the time and that is how I got started." (MC) Mark Cooksey's own comments are denoted (MC).

"I remember this project very well because most of Elite went down to the 20th Cent Fox HQ in London. We had a private pre-release screening of Gremlins II in their mini cinema, kitted out with surround sound. The computer press were invited and Steve Wilcox gave a talk before the film was screened. "I used to love playing this arcade machine when we had got it at the offices at Elite, those Easter Island type stone heads that flew towards you were especially effective. The original in game tune had got a memorable melody so I decided to stick to it. The middle section of my version may be original though, the tune plays a little faster than on the arcade machine. This was due to the fact that my routine didn't contain a fractional timer at that point. Speeds were determined by the shortest note length which could be 1,2,3 or 4 etc. The speed differences were thus 100%, 50,33% etc. with no in between values. The rest of the tunes in the set are original compositions I think, maybe tune 2 was close to the arcade version." "I got the phone call from Mark [Cale] asking me to write some level tunes - I wrote the music, went down there [to System 3] to meet Archer Maclean (? I think it was Arch that put the driver in.....), got offered Mark Cale's slightly-dodgy-import-status left-hand-drive BMW, said "no thanks, I'll have the cash please" and that was that." (BD) Q: How was Anthony Lees to work with? A: "Only met the guy once - on that one day - he said 'hi' - I said 'hi' - that was about it." (BD) The titles of the individual tunes found below are based on as they appear in the game. The Wilderness (loader) Anthony Lees Palace Gardens (loader) Anthony Lees "I did six tunes for LN, the first of which was the one involving the creepy jungle music (....which was and still is my favourite) - the inspiration is hard to nail down, but it was probably the film 'Apocalypse Now' - very dense, troubled and scary moods were evoked." (Anthony Lees) The Wastelands (loader) Ben Daglish The Palace (loader) Anthony Lees The Inner Sanctum (loader) Anthony Lees Interesting comment in this binary: "DONE BY ANTHONY LEES FOR SYSTEM 3 ON 5/4/87...EAT YER HEART OUT GALWAY!". The Wastelands Ben Daglish The Wilderness Ben Daglish Palace Gardens Ben Daglish The Dungeons Anthony Lees The Palace Although the tune is credited to Anthony Lees since 2001 in HVSC, the music player of this tune is by Ben Daglish. Ben doesn't remember making this tune and also he has no idea how the tune ended up being in his player if it was made by Anthony Lees. It could be that the music was credited to Anthony Lees because Anthony claimed to have made 6 tunes for the game while actually 5 are made in his player. Since Anthony passed away, we can't verify it anymore and it will be a mystery who of the two actually made the tune. The Dungeons (loader) Ben Daglish This is also the tune for "The Inner Sanctum". Rubicon, Tune #1 Jeroen Tel "They wanted a title-theme for Shock Magazine, and gave me the first issue. There was a song in there, and I had no clue what it really was but thought it captured the feel of the entire magazine. So I simply made a cover of it, Danko style. I never had any hangups about having to do it all, music is all about sharing and developing ideas together in order to reach higher grounds. The chords aren't identical to Jeroen's version, in fact we had a little thing over that at a party in Oslo back in '94 or so. We hung over a keyboard and I played the chords my style, and he went like 'No! It's like THIS!' and I said 'Well, I want it THIS way!'. *grin* One of the guys at the party leaned over to me and whispered that he in fact preferred my version of the track. *smirk* Jeroen superimposed a sus2 chord throughout the progression until it folds back to the tonic, where the sus2 becomes a m7. It's a nice move, one that I personally use quite a lot myself. But this time around I expanded the progression to plain chords following the bassline. After I had done the tune I found out that it was from Rubicon, but to me it doesn't matter. Later on I made a remix of it, called it Schizomix, with weird sounds. Because Rubicon had been a double-speed song, or something similar, I wanted to make weird and similar sounds but in a single- speed player. And that's all it was, a messed up version of my first cover so to speak." (TD) Tomas Danko's own comments are indicated by (TD).

"I was hanging out on IRC on a regular basis with Waveform. Then he disappeared. I later found out he had terminal cancer. This crushed me to no end. At work I started playing these harmonies on a keyboard (I owned a music store at the time) and it evolved into a song. I wanted him to hear the track to support him in his struggle. Memory eludes me but I do believe he got the word I was making a SID for him and he liked that. He never got to hear the final version. I was completely crushed over this for quite some time. Emulation won't give this track a fair chance, I'm kicking the shit out of old school analog synthesis knowledge and using very slow filter and ringmodulation etc to slowly move through harmonics matching the octaves in sync with the patterns so that the song opens up slowly. This is lost in translation on any emulator." (TD) Tomas Danko's own comments are indicated by (TD).

The corresponding game for this music was never released for the Commodore 64 due to Interplay deciding to shift the game to newer platforms in 1990. Deenen's C64 efforts weren't in vain, however, as he was able to reuse much of the music and began a new phase of his career. In a 2006 posting, Deenen's reflects: "If I hadn't done the C64 Lord of the Rings stuff I wouldn't have gotten my first 'full-time' job in the US. I'd probably be struggling in Holland now trying to make it as a programmer or music guy." "After we got the contract [for Gordian Tomb] with a good value of money, we discussed how to divide it to the people. This was a mess. We at least lost some days of programming. Michael [Detert] was menacing with a dropout if Thomas didn't compose the music. So I thought ok, we are a team and I am busy with programming - why not? But then we couldn't unite about the amount of money. Thomas should get the twice of a normal level for a salary. If I had been a better businessman these days I had done everything by myself, but at least we had a great time and a lot of fun. And the teamwork was always accurate. Finally Thomas had known that the salary was overdrawn and he repaid every dollar with the longest music ever [32:06 minutes] on Commodore 64." (Info from Markus Schneider). "I had no Editor for our Music-Routine at that time, so i was forced to compose and arrange some of my early Game-Tunes with the SOUNDMONITOR. My brother Michael transfered the music data into our Routine while i was drinking lots of coffee in his room. It was a PITA for him and took ages, but it was worth the output." (TD) The original release has a protection which overlaps a fraction of the music data, causing dirty sounds in this tune (most notably, the bass). The game was also released without protection and with correct data, which is present in this rip. Thomas Detert's own comments are denoted (TD).

"Anil [Gupta] asked me to go and meet Roger Gamon. His son had a program called Flight, and they wanted some intro music for it. Anil said to take along some samples. When I arrived, their front room was cluttered with hardware and C64 samplers. I remember saying that I could do with one of those. I took along two sample pieces. One was something in the vein of Those Magnificent Men In Their Flying Machines, which they were really unimpressed with, but the second one rather bowled them over. It was a tune I'd originally written in 1975; I'd found that using the ADSR on a saw channel gave the bass riff an echoey effect, and two pulses slightly detuned from each other played the main theme. I was hired! But I still never got that sampler..." (JD) Julie (née David) Dunn's own comments are denoted (JD).

"The Fourth Protocol was based on a carol I wrote for my school choir, which they performed at Capital Radio in 1979. "I was in a computer shop in Dartford, Kent and I said to someone: 'BASIC is so slow, is there anything that goes faster?' Suddenly, Anil Gupta pops up out of nowhere, literally, and says: 'You need this', handing me what turned out to be a compiler program. I then mentioned that I wrote music, and his eyes started to shine. He asked me to come back once I'd done something in machine code, which I did. It was a demo program made up of some really naff graphics in BASIC, combined with some machined-coded versions of The Mexican Hat Dance, The Thames TV Logo trail and Pipes of Peace. [...] Most importantly, though, Anil was amused." "It was an original. It partly came from the electronic percussion used on the pop tracks of the day, like Ring My Bell, and I thought: 'I can do that'. I re-wrote the whole loader/driver program to make it work. The tune was easy, it had been buzzing around in my head for ages. Thai Boxing was probably the beginning of the end for me: Roger Gamon had since died of a brain tumour, Ocean had enlisted their own in-house programmer, and as the sole contracted person there, I felt I was becoming disinterested." "I wrote it around '84 or '85 as a demo for my music editor called 'Synth'. I was going to University of Waterloo at the time and just gave it to a friend of mine... didn't even bother to put my name on the thing. Anyway it soon started cropping up all over the place. I never made any sequels with music, although there was something with annoying sound effects done in the same style as Synth Sample that I posted in the beginning of 1994. So any music you see that looks like a sequel or has graphics added was done by someone else. Anyway the computer bust of 85/86(?) hit and Synth was never marketed. I had been negotiating with a software company but they went out of business. By that time I was working on a new version of Synth that was a sequencer program for Midi instruments (called MSS), and had joined my first band. I've been in a couple other bands since then, the last one was called SugarPush and we came close to getting signed (but then broke up [...]). So I guess you can credit that little program with launching my musical career..." (GF) Theme from A Stationary Ark John Mills-Cockell "Theme from Stationary Ark, a nature show on PBS. [...] It appears on Synth Sample as interpreted by a friend of mine. I didn't know what it was myself until I happened to see Stationary Ark one time. This song does not play properly on some C-64's where the SID chip filter is calibrated differently." This is the very first published tune on the C64 that used samples. "Q: How did you get involved with using sampled sounds? I figured out how samples were played by hacking into someone else's code... OK, I admit it... It was a drum synthesizer package called Digidrums, actually, so you could still say I was the first to include samples in a piece of music. [...] Never would I claim to have invented that technique, I just got it published first. In fact, I couldn't really figure out where they got the sample data, just that they were wiggling the volume register, so I tried to make up my own drum sample sounds in realtime - which is the flatulence stuff that shipped in 'Arkanoid'. [...] After the project was in the shops I gained access to some real drum samples, and I slid those into my own custom version of the tune. The one that's in the shops is kind of a collage of farts & burps, don't you think? [...] Later I was able to acquire some proper drum samples and by 'Game Over' it got quite sophisticated." (MG) Cobra (Title) [from the Spectrum game] Martin Galway "I'm glad you spotted 'Cobra' on the Spectrum, whose tune I was in love with and HAD to use somewhere else...! I figured no-one would complain if I used it a year later [for Arkanoid] on the C64." "The Miami Vice game was a very quick job. I had been handed 'Miami Vice' and 'Highlander' because the outside development team working on it hadn't worked out who was going to do the sound (notice those games have little or no sound-effects), so I did my best in a very short time. I [...] picked 'The Chase' and the 'Main Theme' as the two tunes I would do. We had settled on two modes for the game - in your car and out of it I think. (Or maybe it was in the game and out of it, I can't remember.) I started on 'The Chase' and if you listen to the first few seconds of that you can hear the basis of that super-filter-echo tune that is so cool. I recall David Collier was sitting in the office with me while I was working on it. But while messing with it while everyone else was at lunch, I came across this cool sound. I added to it and added to it, and when we applied the non-sync'd filter sweep we both flipped out! I decided to abandon the conversion of that tune and simply go with the cool sounds I had stumbled upon. When the guys came back from lunch and listened to it they swore that there was a cassette deck connected somewhere and it wasn't the C64 playing it! Such a sound had not been heard before by any of us out of the C64. So I extended it and turned it into this tripping-out 11-minute piece. The main theme itself... I simply did my best with no drums (Rob Hubbard's strength). I think my strength with guitar solos helped pull it off. Both of those problematic games benefited from my music, actually, and the Ocean management were very relieved (understatement)." Before starting on this game Galway bought Rendez-Vous (by Jean Michel Jarre). He listened to it daily. His CD player broke 2 weeks later and didn't get repaired for 2 months, during which time Martin worked on Parallax, without realizing that Rendez-Vous was unconsciously creeping into the music. He realized it only after he played the album again after the game was already shipped. "[Parallax] was 11 minutes long, certainly my longest at the time. I took my development gear home to work on it for a week or two. I just said to myself 'OK, it's going to be this mega-tune, so the intro has to be mega'. The intro took up two-thirds of the tune! I actually got bored with it, and stuck that silly melody on the end which doesn't really match. Going back I would have made it less melodic. I wanted to reflect the gigantic visual proportions represented by the parallax effect in the game so that's why it has an 'epic' feel."(MG) Rendez-Vous [from Rendez-Vous] Jean-Michel Jarre Martin Galway's own comments are denoted (MG). "I believe it to be my most elaborate, complete and successful conversion of a 'digital audio sourced' tune. ZZAP! 64 only gave the music 79%, my worst score since 'Roland's Rat Race', so you can imagine my disappointment. One of the other tunes was easy, that's the simple ballad melody 'come and follow me', which I was able to arrange quite successfully. "Of course I have recollections... where do I begin... are you sitting comfortably? The fact that there are two versions of Streethawk music is part of the whole mystery of Streethawk, really. It started in 1985 and was programmed by Mike Webb, who'd just come off Amstrad Kong Strikes Back. Lateral thinker that he is, he had a rather unique design going (a sideways scrolling platform-jumping design which is probably now lost forever), and I think he went on holiday for a week or two, and when he came back they decided to have him do another project - or, he left to join forces with Richard Kay at Software Creations. (He definitely did the latter, but I can't remember the timeline exactly.)" (MG) Le Parc (Theme to Street Hawk) [from Le Parc] Tangerine Dream This is a re-interpreted cover by Galway. "I had done music for Mike Webb's version of the game, simply taking a stab at the title screen music without doing anything else. I did it some time in the summer of 1985, so it sonically resembles Cyclone/Helicopter Jagd and Neverending Story. There was no filter technology in my driver. All that Ocean had as reference for the show was an NTSC tape of the pilot episode of the series, which we were able to play on our futuristic, highly-technical NTSC-playback VCR/TV. By listening to the opening & closing credits, I put the tune in by ear." (MG) Martin Galway's own comments are denoted (MG). "The game was re-assigned in early 1986 to Comic Bakery's programmer Colin Gresty and artist Steve Wahid, and they enthusiastically got to work on it, coming up with an all-new approach with nicer graphics - more like the early Grand Theft Auto games (top-down viewed from a chase camera). However it was very slow going for those guys and while the art/design was done by mid-1987, Colin was still finishing the programming towards the end of that year, say, about September. Ocean, who'd been advertising the game in magazines for months, were very annoyed by this delay and were not going to make their intended profit. (Perhaps their option window to publish the game was expiring too, who knows?) So they cancelled the project when it was at the 99%-complete stage and fired Colin." (MG) The tune names shown are what Galway called them in his source code. Le Parc (Theme to Street Hawk) [from Le Parc] Tangerine Dream This is a re-interpreted cover by Galway. "When I did the 2nd pass at [Street Hawk], I simply bookended the old [prototype] version with new stuff, using all my latest techniques. If I remember correctly this was the first complete tune I did with a proper filter control - perhaps a short time before Wizball. I also incorporated that weird sound from the Parallax walking around subtune, where two waveform bits are set simultaneously. So... you'll hear a bunch of fat, juicy filtered bass w/ cool textures, a thinner middle bit, then more phat stuff on the end." (MG) EnterName The High-score entry music. "I tried to create this feeling of a massive behemoth robot monster on its way to destroy you. Thus the marching beat and the minor chords and stark tones. I had to stick in the inevitable jamming solo towards the end of course. I was starting to face the glass ceiling imposed by the filter on the C64. While my particular SID sounded great, others were not like it at all and the solos were almost inaudible! At the other extreme the new C64C's were coming out and this filter unreliability had been fixed as part of a silicon revision. BUT the filters were way too open all the time and you could hardly hear any filtering! This caused the filtered note to come out a lot louder than it should have and 'stick out' rather unattractively. So I developed a 'filter adjustment' parameter for my music program which would allow the customer to control this filter unreliability and get their particular machine to sound cool. But David Collier never put it in the options screen. (DOH!) There's always something wrong, eh?" The opening bars of this tune are sampled by the group Console on their song "14 Zero Zero". "I was working at the Sensible Software office at the time of the major music creation, but the title screen music never got finished. When I returned to Ocean I got on with some other things, all the time worrying about this unfinished tune. Finally I slapped something on the end of it. I knew I could never top the first part, that's what the problem was. In my mind the second part of the tune is pretty lame compared with the first part. But for some people it represents the mysterious, magical, unconventional aspect of 'Wizball' so it fits in some ways. But you can tell it's not really like the other music in the game, which was primarily developed when I was with the Sensi boys, basking in that Sensi VIBE." (MG) "I really worked on the sound design of the voices a lot. The music seems to "flow" and "breathe" unlike anything before it." (MG) "Tune #5, the bonus screen tune, consists of several short riffs, and John Hare came up with the most musical ones on his bass guitar. I remember he would come up with the riffs, playing them over and over at full volume on his band's P.A. in their rented terraced house in Southend (not caring about what the neighbours thought!!!) - and while they went out to get me a "blow-out" burger at 3am, I would be transcribing it and enhancing it (a little)." (MG) "I composed the high-score music at Ocean after returning from Southend. Played it on the synth keyboard there. It's one of the few compositions of mine that I can actually play a decent rendition of on the piano." (MG) "Chris Yates wrote the game over riff on his electric guitar. They were pretty impressed by the translation when they came back with my blow-out." (MG) Martin Galway's own comments are denoted (MG). "I just tried to come up with a crazy way of settling on a beginning note (my favourite beginning note of course, G - almost everything I do is in G). So I plugged in this echoing waveform thing and let it rip. The tune isn't particularly Chinese sounding, but I was working on producing that 'perfect melody', the one you'd be humming all day, you know. That was a phase I went through. [...] The sound I was converting from was itself a conversion of the arcade cabinet, which I have NEVER SEEN. It sounded like it was a lame conversion too, so I easily did a better sounding version. (The MSX's music only used two notes at once, for example.)" (MG) The MSX version of the game was the original release on cartridge in 1985. Therefore Martin Galway's recollection is covering the MSX release, as this game did not get an arcade release. Tension [from the game YS] Yuzo Koshiro "The original is a chiptune I found in the '.m' format, which is compiled MML code (Music Markup Language). "Sometime in November 1987, I got a phone call from Mark Cale of System 3 Software, asking if I could provide a loading track for Bangkok Knights, but they needed it next week. Rob had done the in-game, but I think he was departing for the US and didn't have time to do another track. This was a big opportunity, to effectively stand in for my SID hero. There was also the tempting prospect of perhaps working on the sequel to The Last Ninja the following year. I went up to their Hampstead offices in London the following week with my loading track for Bangkok Knights. Mark listened to it and approved it, then we went for a drink, where he offered me an exclusive contract to work for System 3. I said yes, and that was that. In mid-January of 1988, I started work on The Last Ninja 2." (MDG) Matt Gray's own comments are denoted (MDG).

This is the sequel to Stormlord. "The story about the music for Stormlord II is long and tiresome, but to make it short I can say that Hewson never was satisfied with whatever Charles Deenen had to offer. Laxity, Reyn Ouwehand, Johannes Bjerregaard, Charles Deenen, Jeroen Tel, Jesper Olsen and even Link tried to do the music for the game, but Hewson always rejected it, and finally chose Matt Grey as the correct composer..." (Comment by JCH, from the demo "Vibrants Screens") Other versions can be found in the following directories: Bjerregaard_Johannes, JO, Laxity, Link, and Ouwehand_Reyn. "In 1990, I produced Deliverance: Stormlord II, my last ever SID track. Ironically, it was for Hewson Consultants, who folded soon after. It was time for a change, and by then I was starting to release dance music for club play. It's an alright piece of work, though I think the sounds were probably better than some of the tunes. I've just reworked it for a Kickstarter project and it sounds so much better now." (MDG) Also used in the unreleased game "Hyperion 2", (C) 1988 Technical Solitude, with slightly differences. "Driller, which I did for Incentive Software, was another big turning point for me. They wanted something long and epic, not short and repetitive. Concept-wise, it was the perfect game for me. It was exactly the sort of thing I had been waiting to get my teeth into musically. It took four weeks to complete, including an almost two-week pause in the middle when the Great Storm of 1987 struck the UK, leaving us without electricity or heating for about ten or eleven days. I can remember walking down our road one dark evening, wondering if I would ever get to use the C64 again, and suddenly noticing all the neighbours' lights were finally on again. I went straight in, fired up the assembler and carried on composing." (MDG) This is how the game plays the tune, much faster than intended. In the game the tune was synced up to the Keyboard interrupts, speeding it up and making it two minutes shorter. "In 1988, as mentioned, I did The Last Ninja 2 for System 3. I did the Central Park tracks first, which was important in order to stamp some sort of "sound" on the game. It basically took from mid-January until early April to finish. It's about as big a project as you would want to undertake, but everything just seemed to work without any real hitches. I was given a fairly free hand to produce what I thought would be most suitable and luckily, every time I took in new tracks for each level, I got the thumbs up. It was a great time for me personally, to suddenly be working full time on C64 music. I was almost 18, but I had no real worries in the world beyond whether I could afford to buy a better car. I think the entire The Last Ninja 2 soundtrack is my proudest achievement, especially the Central Park tracks, as they seem to mean so much to so many people. The project itself was a pleasure to be part of. The whole team involved were probably at the top of their C64 game at the time, from John's programming to Hugh's fantastic graphics, Tim's storyboarding and of course Mark's overall vision and commitment. It's amazing that we're still talking about it nearly 30 years on." "Released in 1992, made with ALD-player v3.0 which was developed late 1990. The routine turned out to be the one I used most, though v3.7 was even ready at the time. The tune itself was the first one I was asked to do for a game. ATA was a Tetris-clone done by German Lower Level and I don't recall if I got paid for the track, but anyway it was liked by the authors and apparently many others. This must have been the best track I've done if I don't take count on my new tunes. I wasn't anymore much into composing that time, I just composed as a time-killer. This was an early working version of the music from Monty on the Run. The programmers asked Rob to do a version of the Dick Barton theme, and then needed the tune changing before the game was released. The time stamps below are when it's an exact one to one version. "I found this code during research on Rob's drivers for his biography. It was present in the demo code but wasn't referenced from the menu, and had half its driver missing (Rob Hubbard demos tended to have multiple drivers). However, the patches and tune data were intact and could be successfully played back through the existing Thing on a Spring driver." (Chris Abbott) "OK this is twilight zone stuff! I do remember transcribing the tune note for note, since that's what they actually asked for, but I don't recall ever coding it up, or putting it into a demo. After I transcribed it, I straight away set about making all the changes to please them, and get round any rights issues. Maybe I did code up Galop, and gave Gremlin a demo, and then was asked to do a pastiche." "Human Race was a very interesting project. The tunes tried to capture some of the feel of the game, evolution etc... One of the tunes was also used for an ST game (GoldRunner I think). I only used 2 SID voices for all these tunes because I used the other for SFX...... Most of the tunes were sketched out on a small keyboard and manuscript paper. I used paper to keep track of the basic ideas and arrangement, and I still have all the original manuscripts. A lot of the manuscripts are not readable because I used to work very fast and never updated many of the changes I made. I used to use a machine code monitor to edit music data and sound patch data on the file while the tune was playing. This allowed me to really fine tune the SID parameters for the music." "Last V8 was a simple futuristic game and so I was off into Jarre land.... I purposely wrote the 2 melody lines to work off one voice to make it sound like more than 1 voice." (RH) The Last V8 was the first game released by Mastertronic's new label MAD (Mastertronic's Added Dimension). Review copies of this game had a bugged loader which mucked up the music and so reviewers of the game gave the music a much lower rating. Julian Rignall (ex-editor of Zzap! 64) takes up the story: "I remember the God awful cacophony that was our review copy of Thrust's music as though it were still playing. This was the problem: the drum sounds worked, but all the other instrument sounds were screwed - basically it resulted in this horrible screeching noise playing to drums, rather than the cool heavyish sound that was heard in the final version of the game. It sounded really harsh and so it was duly shot down by us in the review. I remember hearing the 'proper' version of the game at a later dater and thinking 'ooooops!'. After all it was a classic tune (it became one of my faves, indeed) and we'd mercilessly beaten it down in the review, which was totally unfair. Still, it was good to be able to do a ZZAPback on it and remedy the error." People have often stolen Hubbard's routine causing some tunes to be falsely credited to him. Very interesting story here. Katakis was released in September 1988 by Rainbow Arts, however it never got a release in the UK as Activision had it cancelled because of similarities to R-Type, to which Activision had bought the conversion rights. Activision were getting nowhere with their conversion of R-Type and they liked what they saw of Katakis, so they hired the same programming team (Manfred Trenz and others) to do the C64 conversion. They only got 6 weeks to write the conversion, and sadly, it shows. Katakis was eventually altered and released as Denaris in 1989. Tunes #2 to #14 all cover of the arcade game. Although SoundMonitor had arrived at that point, I didn't like it much and thus never considered using it." (JCH)

entries.s: "Ray kept saying "Make more mutispeed music", so I did. Actully, it only runs channel #1 at 63x, the other two channels run at 9x, but oh well :). And it's too short... I very quickly got annoyed with the unresponsiveness of the editor when trying to play sounds at this rate. But I *do* like working with the sounds at these sort of update rates, so I'm working on a player which takes a smaller amount of raster time than TFX to use for such music. (That said, one of PCH's TFX songs (supposedly) runs a channel at 72x, but that's just too insane to dicuss :)." (JJ) "Many people change their scene name once or twice in their life. I decided to be different, and change my real name instead. "(JJ)

"Someone on c64.sk made the statement that to do well, you need to make songs which only use the triangle wave. So I did, and I think it sounds a lot like something you'd hear on a NES. I actually prefer this version myself." (JJ) "Many people change their scene name once or twice in their life. I decided to be different, and change my real name instead. "(JJ)

"The title of this song comes from my friend Jenn's AIM screenname, whom I love dearly (in a completly plutonic way, for the record). She doesn't understand the 'c64 thing'. I always wanted to be able to write funk tunes like Drax, and later Mitch&Dane, do, and despite it coming almost dead last in the c64.sk SID competition, I think I succeeded somewhat. I actually like a lot of the harmonic work in this song, as did my sister, who yelled at me after she first heard it for being able to pull it off! Of course, most people disagreed with her accusation of me pulling it off." (JJ) "Many people change their scene name once or twice in their life. I decided to be different, and change my real name instead. "(JJ)
"Many people change their scene name once or twice in their life. I decided to be different, and change my real name instead. "(JJ)

Blood, Starlight, Rain Like Tears. "Sitting in a backpackers hostel in sydney, get a call from my parents, I can't come home, they've rented out my room. I've been here for 5 weeks now, but only finally got a laptop this day. I was feeling incredibly dark, having spent the last week in bed ill, I really wanted to go home, or failing that, I wanted someone to take a few minutes out of their day to see if I was still alive (okay, so I was feeling kind of melodramatic, lol), This girl promised to hang out with me, and then cancelled or forgot every time for weeks straight, and I was stupid (read: thinking with my heart instead of my head) and didn't want to acknowlage that she was ignoring me... I was losing my mind, and this music represents that. The full verse is "Blood, Starlight, Rain like tears, Drink from this, and let go the years". I don't know who penned those words, but I dropped the latter half from the title because I promised said girl that I would. This music was made on an emulator (vice 1.8, and of course I had resid turned on :-p). It was also one of my bigger expermients with filters synced from different channels to the one they're targetting. If it works at all on a real C64, I'd consider myself very lucky, lol, because I didn't have access to one at the time." (JJ) "Many people change their scene name once or twice in their life. I decided to be different, and change my real name instead. "(JJ)

The second half is mostly an experiment in what happens when you mix diffrent types of Ringmod and Sync effects, which I like the sound of. Sidplay1 hates it. It was originally intended to sound quite different from this, because the original sketch for it required a dyanmic wave table, but I got fed up waiting for that, and finished it as is." "I try, I fly, I lie, I cry, I die. My mis-understood epic. Everyone except for Ray hated this :). It started out as soundmon clone music (intended for the WOW demo of the same name), an evolution in music, you know, the idea being that I've also got future composer type music (see TFX == future composer), and the other guys were going to do modern music blah blah watever, I forget the details. Anyhow, around 2 minutes after I sat down at the editor, it instead became something else (I hate it when that happens :-p), which basically amounts to an attempt to place what was goes through my mind at the time into SID form... the evolution of my soul. I achieved that, I think, which is probably why almost no-one else understands it. I personally like this music better than any other which I have ever made, however my emotional attachment to it makes me biased." [from the GG game Sonic 2] Masafumi Ogata "I beat this game in a couple of hours when it first came out, but always loved the music, and this tune in particular. Fast forward to mid 2000, and I'm sitting in a backpackers hostel in Prague with my gamegear, and I have no alarm clock and a 9am flight to catch, with my girlfriend (who I hadn't seen for 5 months) is waiting on the other end of it. So hence I can't really go to sleep (I'd die if I missed said flight :-p), but hey, I have a gamegear with this game, and so I play until Green Hill zone, and then listen to this music for 7 hours straight, at which point I finally ran out of spare lives and continues. Fast forward to June/July 2001, and I've got some weird illness where I can't stand up or hold down food (never did work out what the was, heh), and my girlfriend runs away to america because the idea that for once in her life she has to be an adult is to damned hard to deal with (Hey, Gundam Wing Hentai is much more fun), and I havn't slept for 2 weeks or eaten in 4 weeks (not an exaggeration), which has had the predictable effects on my mind. Crawl over to my C64, load TFX, bury myself of memories of that night in Prague and happy fun music! Only digital love is eternal." (JJ) "Many people change their scene name once or twice in their life. I decided to be different, and change my real name instead. "(JJ)

Maybe one day I'll remake it and release it, because the ideas in it were good, just bad implentation as is the usual thing with me :). It wasn't until later that year the the message penetrated my brain that, if you want to make an okay music, you need to spend more than an hour on it ;). If I was running WOW, I would have kicked me out for being completly lame ;). But hey, I learned my lesson (sort of....)" (JJ) "Many people change their scene name once or twice in their life. Midi Drums [from the midi module] Jaymz Julian "This is the second attempt I made to do this song on the C64, and was in fact the song that TFX table variables were created for. I originally tried to do this in Sid Duzz It in early 1999, but the number of arpeggio commands required for the places where there is two leads in one channel, and the blips in the drum/bass channel, overwelmed that editor. So I tried in JCH v20g4, where I had managed to succed with Sunset Spirals, due to the ability it has to change the wavetable from within a song, but this too was not to be, due to the limitations of the editor. So, I started writing a new editor, which was specifically designed to handle this situation, by splitting each channel into six virtual channels, and using special rules to modulate them together. But this took up a lot of ram and raster time, indeed it too so much ram in the editor that I could only store five patterns at a time, so this was not to be either. So Ray introduced me to TFX, and I asked him about changing the wave table from within the song, but he wouldn't have this, because it would confuse people, but he suggested a viable alternative, which is to support variables in the wave table, and promised to add this feature asap. That was January 2001, but he was too busy to implement them for the next two and a half years. So I started bugging him to just give me the source and the bits to build it, and in November 2003, he did. So, I put my money where my mouth was, and added that feature (and a bunch of others which I had been wanting for a long time), and I was _finally_ able to do a version of this that I happy with. To anyone else but me, this is just another mediocre game tune, but for me it was an achievement." (JJ) "Many people change their scene name once or twice in their life. (JJ) "Many people change their scene name once or twice in their life. I decided to be different, and change my real name instead. "(JJ)

Purple Sky II [from the Scream Tracker 3 module] Jonne Valtonen (Purple Motion) "After Sunset Sprirals, I was once again fed up with JCH's editor, and wanted something better. Ray had suggested to me using TFX several times before, and I finally got some documentation for it, and so now was the time to use it. I had the S3M of this kicking around, and so I covered it to learn the editor. The instruments suck... I never was good at making percussion, and unfortunantly there isn't any good ones around made in TFX to rip. I also had basically zero understanding of how the wave tables worked when I did this, and as a result there are some very stupid things in there which sound terrible ;). This probably should never have been released, but people liked it for reasons that I don't understand. As it turned out, the instruments sounded so crap partially because Ray's player was horrifically bugged, at the time. I recompiled it against a later player, and it sounds a LOT better." (JJ) "Many people change their scene name once or twice in their life. I decided to be different, and change my real name instead. "(JJ)

Flop Magazine 41 [from the Atari XL/XE music] Radek Sterba (Raster) "So, TFX 2.9 still wasn't here, but I wanted to cover this 4 channel music from the atari, so what I did, is set the player to 1 frame per row, and then enter all of the arpeggios by hand. I'm surprised it didn't make the file much larger than it is. It was a pain in the ass, but I'm quite pleased with the result." (JJ) "Many people change their scene name once or twice in their life. I decided to be different, and change my real name instead. "(JJ)

"This song is made up entirely of patterns from Fishmagic, but played a different tempo's and in a differnet order. It was originally intended to be used in a demo with fishmagic, so I was going for that similar but different effect, and I think it worked very well. But, ironically, I was never happy enough with the original fishmagic, or how the demo was turning out, so I gave this to Jazzcat for an issue of Vandalism News, for which it was much more suitable anyhow. I love this sort of song, why don't people do more of them?" (JJ) "Many people change their scene name once or twice in their life. I decided to be different, and change my real name instead. "(JJ)

"This was my entry for the 2004 SidWine competition, and it did fantasitcally badly, despite being what I consider to be probably the best demoscene style song that I've done on the C64. I actually spent a lot of time on this song, and I was quite proud of how it turned out when it was finished. It makes extensive use of the TFX wave table variables to try and squeeze two melody lines into a single channel, and the NoPulse command to control pulse width modulation reset more finely. The song is dedicated to a group I used to be a part of, Sonic Dreams, which is another story." (JJ) "Many people change their scene name once or twice in their life. Sunset Spirals [from the Impulse Tracker module] Jaymz Julian (A Life in Hell) "This is, musically, probably the best thing that I have ever done on the C64. Ironically, all of my C64 friends complained that it was off key, etc, and all of my PC friends love this version. Yet I had exactly the opposite reaction to the original version (c64 guys tended to like it, pc guys tended to complain that it was off key.). For the record, except for one or two notes, because I ran out of arpeggios (I do that a lot... there are two or three other musics which got scrapped half way through because I ran out of arpeggios. Thankfully, we've come up with a solution to this in the new version of TFX :)), the notes are NOT off key, and I don't care what you all think :-p. Said PC guys decided to take ownership of this song, and wanted me to create more like it, but I havn't had the motivation to actully finish any of them. (There are many, many, many stories that I could tell about the digiradi guys, but that's for another day, but the credit of the music to "Coder" is a part of that insanity. They were great times)." (JJ) "Many people change their scene name once or twice in their life. I decided to be different, and change my real name instead. "(JJ)

"The Tim in question is Tim Bray, who does an act "Casionova", where he shows off 80's home keyboards, and other chip instruments, including a Commodore 64 with a guitar strap attached. Loscha and I were at one of his gigs, and he was tanking really badly (indeed, we could remember more of the words to his songs than he could!). This was mostly because, we think, he was completly off the planet. So, we came back to my place, after the gig, and I was showing off the new version of TFX, and we wrote the bass/chord/drum line (which is all one channel) to demonstrate some of the new features. The file needed a name, and so we just typed in "Tim got high", and the name stuck. This song also has a lot of ring modulation (Joxstrap/WOW said too much :-p), which I love as always." (JJ) "Many people change their scene name once or twice in their life. I decided to be different, and change my real name instead. "(JJ)

Winter's Dream [from the Impulse Tracker module] Andrew Sega (Necros) "Back when I was writing music on the PC for 16 hours a day, every day, this was the demo song included with one of the many "this is the last release really!" releases of impulse tracker. I'd actually wanted to make a C64 version of this for a long time, but it took me until now to really work out how to do it to my liking. Throwing that piece of junk away to concentrate on C64 music was the best descision I ever made. I never was very good at it, anyhow." (JJ) "Many people change their scene name once or twice in their life. I decided to be different, and change my real name instead. "(JJ)

"This is the only released music made in the modified version of JCH's player that I was hacking up during 1999 (I had all of my stuff stolen, including the only copy of the player sources etc). I originally wanted to create Galway style tune, but changed my mind half way and thought I'd make a Drax style music instead, and then put a JCH style lead on it. Read the title backwards, and it will all make sense. This was also the first music of mine that I know of to be used in someone else's production (of course *I* use my own music, but well, it's crap, so no-one else does), which was a graphic collection by someone in Sonic Dreams (Rat I think). Those guys were great fun, and some of them actully liked my music, which was a nice change, but goddamn the organisation of that group turned into a clusterfuck :-p, But it was all fun at the end of the day." (JJ) "Many people change their scene name once or twice in their life. I decided to be different, and change my real name instead. "(JJ)

Ryo Kawasaki's own comments are denoted (RK). "When the first time Commodore 64 computer hit the market in 1983, I rushed to buy it by paying $600 at some electronic store on 45th street in Manhattan. It was 8-bit with only 64KB of memory. Then I spent two years to write these four programs as well as unpublished Midi-Workstation (8-track real-time Midi recorder) all by machine code using SuperMon without assembler so that it runs fast and leave enough memory for music data. Each of these programs was sold for $49.95 in retail stores furnished with handsome package came with 5-inch floppy disk and manual. In 15 years, now we can buy 1GHz PC for the same price as I bought my first C64. And I wonder what kind of computer we can buy 15 years from now by paying $600?" (RK) Sadly, Ryo Kawasaki passed away on April 13th, 2020 at the age of 73.

Then I spent two years to write these four programs as well as unpublished Midi-Workstation (8-track real-time Midi recorder) all by machine code using SuperMon without assembler so that it runs fast and leave enough memory for music data. Each of these programs was sold for $49.95 in retail stores furnished with handsome package came with 5-inch floppy disk and manual. In 15 years, now we can buy 1GHz PC for the same price as I bought my first C64. And I wonder what kind of computer we can buy 15 years from now by paying $600?" (RK) Sadly, Ryo Kawasaki passed away on April 13th, 2020 at the age of 73.

"This demonstrates a new method of playing back digitized samples. It demonstrates the output of my new audio encoder that produces output that is able to be decoded on the C64 using only a few raster lines per frame. It uses the free running SID oscillators on the C64's SID chip in 3 channels and a master volume to recreate the audio. Mainly suited for speech, but can also work on other sources. This demonstration packs a few minutes of audio into less than 47k and running in a C64 made in the early 80's with only 1MHz processor." Hoodoo Voodoo Graham Marsh (BOGG) "Icups - my first published work... I had written the tune as a demo, and I had been trading with Bogg for a few years, and I had re-written his tune just to see how I would have taken his initial idea and run with it myself. Anyways, I had sent disks with a load of tunes on to all the major software companies at the time. Firebird contacted me, they wanted to use Icups. I told them at the time that it was kind of a rip off of Bogg's Detergent, but they were quite happy to offer to buy it. They offered me 150 pounds, and then when someone pointed out again to them that it was based on Bogg's tune, they gave him half the money too which I was quite happy with." (BL) All Barry's comments are indicated by (BL).

"The tune is remarkable from a technical point of view, because the playroutine only needs 63 clock cycles (one rasterline) per frame, whereas a normal playroutine needs around 24 rasterlines. To put that in perspective, consider that simply calling the playroutine (jump to subroutine + return from subroutine) uses up 12 cycles, i.e. almost 20% of the available time. Obviously this severely limits the number of features the player can support; there's no vibrato, no arpeggios, and so on. Still, it was fun to try to work musically within those extreme constraints. This project then went on to inspire Hermit Soft to create One Rasterline Tracker, a tool that lets non-coders take part in the fun. However, his playroutine is not quite down to 63 cycles yet, and believe me, the last few are the hardest. Still, it's a great achievement!" (LA) Lft's (Linus Akesson) own comments are denoted (LA)

Allt under himmelens fäste Visa Röster "At a concert where Visa Röster interpreted both SID tunes and Swedish folk songs, my girlfriend and I bought a couple of CDs, and found a little gem called Allt under himmelens fäste that we both instantly liked. It's a very sad song with a simple melody, supported by a solemn yet rhythmical accompaniment written by Mahoney. If you're a SID composer, you know that when you get a song stuck on your mind, it inevitably ends up as a SID tune. =) In this case, I've tried to stick to Mahoney's arrangement as far as possible." "I composed this SID tune for the Executable Music Oldskool compo at Revision 2014, where it ended up on 5th place. This piece is a genre study: It is heavily inspired by the kind of lyrical and highly energetic J-pop that tends to be used as opening themes for Anime series. During the (anonymised) compo some people speculated that this was a cover song. This is nice to hear, because it means that I managed to capture the lyrical style well. My conclusion from the experiment is that the genre works well with 8-bit sounds." (LA) Lft's (Linus Akesson) own comments are denoted (LA)

Since having no sequencer or other audio gear except my Roland M5, I started doing c64 SIDs using a program called AMP. It allowed to compose in a tracker-like environment, and had a nice interface for creating sounds. I tried to learn several techniques by covering Hubbard's Commando, but my best SID was a cover of Moroder's Midnight Express." (LMan)

The Great Giana Sisters, Tune #1 Chris Hülsbeck Remake of "Giana Sisters DS - Title Theme", by Fabian del Priore, from the Nintendo DS version of the game released in 2009. "This is a remake of the beautiful title tune from Giana Sisters for the Nintendo DS, released 2009. The tune was composed and arranged by Fabian del Priore aka Rapture, and is itself a cover of Chris Hülsbeck's original Giana Sisters Title Theme. I contacted Rapture about my intent to recreate the tune on a stock c64. He liked the idea and kindly provided the original audio source files. My challenge was to port every little detail from the original and make it fit the limits given by the c64's hardware. The music engine was coded by THCM, with the SID part done in CheeseCutter, and the sample part in OpenMPT." (LMan)

SW1.9-EMU "The Shadow introduced me to Zarko who was working on a C64 game project called Bricks'n'Walls, under Avatar flag. Zarko is a very cool and humbe guy with an awesome work ethic so we quickly got along well. His game project was a tribute to wallbreaker games like Krakout or Arkanoid. Out of respect, we agreed on adding a couple of tune covers of legendary wallbreaker music to the game project. It includes a lot of subtunes. The ingame ones were tricky as they had to be 2-channel as the 3rd channel was reserved for sound FX. The audio engine that provided all (+SFX) was SID-Wizard 1.9 tracker by Hermit who also offered some very good tech assistance on the way. About composing, all of the songs were recorded with a MIDI keyboard, arranged inside Reaper DAW and exported as 3-channel MIDI. The SWMconvert.exe turned it into 3-channel note data for SID-Wizard where the sounds became added / tweaked and the data assigned to subtunes. Using a MIDI converter is a very fast process. This way, the whole project took about the same time as feeding music data to a tracker manually for a single tune would." (NP) Menu Expectations Too High [from From A to B through Z EP] NecroPolo "SID cover of the original 2012 rock version." The tune itself is of course SID-Wizard and MIDI conversion. Around the time of creation (spring 2021) I believed that it will be released in weeks so I shot a video of the tracker, timed it on Youtube and forgot about it. As it turned out the demo itself became released much later (November-something?) so the audio became accidentally leaked on Youtube around May. Oooops..." (NP) NecroPolo's own comments are denoted (NP).

Virtuoso 1.02 "Despite that Virtuoso is a very nice tool, it is not my tool. You have to keep a rather big number of cross references of various tables in mind compared to other tackers that means an ample of tiny calculations. Well, I am really bad at calculations. I always make mistakes. So composing was like 20% of composing and 80% of fixing my bad calculations. As a consequence the tune for this C64GTC round became very short and simple." (NP) NecroPolo's own comments are denoted (NP).

The Raid [from the Amiga game Defender of the Crown] (0:00) Jim Cuomo The Saxon Maid [from the Amiga game Defender of the Crown] (1:47) Jim Cuomo NT2.03 "Shortly after my SID remix album 'rakBIT' was released including a remix of Richard's brilliant 'Rimrunner', Jazzcat contacted me and asked to join the Richard Joseph (R.I.P.) tribute demo project with a C64 remake of one of Richard's great SIDs, a tune of my choice. It's been an honour to be invited: I respect Richard and admire his works much, not to mention the fine array of SID composers who also contributed to the demo. This remake was made in a rather short time and it includes very old ideas of mine that are rooted back in '89. The SID was named after the guitar that I used to grab the notes." (NP) Covers /MUSICIANS/J/Joseph_Richard/Defender_of_the_Crown.sid, Tunes #7 and #10. NecroPolo's own comments are denoted (NP).

GT2.7 "Entry for Didi's cracktro music compo. It uses the least possible number of blocks that make a tune to me. It was among the first ones I created with GoatTracker2 around 2009, unreleased until the 2013 compo." (NP) NecroPolo's own comments are denoted (NP).

GMC1.6 "These little jingles were created for a retro race game project for iPhone in 2010 that haven't reached the finish line so far. All were extracted from full length audio tracks and full-size SID tunes. Project is just iced but not completely aborted so depending on it I'll see what the future of the full tunes will be." (NP) Game over "Similar to a famous Top Gun movie track but not a cover" (NP) Coastal lvl intro Citly lvl intro Canyon lvl intro Danger '64 jingle Danger Zone [from the movie Top Gun] Giorgio Moroder & Tom Whitlock, performed by Kenny Loggins "Similar to a famous Top Gun movie track but not a cover" (NP) NecroPolo's own comments are denoted (NP).

GMC2.0 "1991 GMC1.6 worktune optimised and finished with GMC2.0 as a compliment for AGod's funny ninja picture for X2010. Title means Lucky Bunny in Chinese as far as I know." (NP) NecroPolo's own comments are denoted (NP).

SW1.8 "A test tune for Hermit's SIDwizard 1.8 release that is maybe a little rough around the edges. During test I was split between being on tour and my normal job so I had just a day or two to check this superb tracker before release. Shame on me. About this tune, the title and the idea comes from a little friendly discussion back in my jazz college days, with a Mr. All-Know type of music theory guy. Too much music theory will zap your brain, all I can tell you. Using your f'n insticnt is still the best." (NP) NecroPolo's own comments are denoted (NP).

GMC1.6 "My second (and last) game tune back in the time, created for an odd software developer called zOnE. Geister was a minimalistic and badass turn-based sci-fi strategy, a bit similar to Laser Squad. All the source code was destroyed when zOnE's place burnt to dust in October, 1994. zOnE stopped writing games and I stopped writing C64 music afterwards. Some riffs of Geister survived in my later band projects. This collection was onefiled by iAN CooG, packing together independent workfiles." (NP) All tunes are made in 1994, released in 2009. Intro Start/title screen Reactor level F'n big droid level Scanner level "There is some off-beat "beep" for zOnE's request as a scanner-like sound. That was zOnE's fav track, especially the concrete breaker part from 1:30." (NP) Abductor level Dreadnought level "Riffs from this subtune were used in the first Wackor EP in 1999 in the song 'Iced'." (NP) Time out! /last turn/ "zOnE wanted an annoying little tunelet that alarms the player that he has mere seconds (one turn) until next failure. I guess, that's fulfilled :)" (NP) Level complete "Riffs were used in the first RKH album in 1995 in the song "Curable". I wrote the whole song around that little piece." (NP) Weapon shop "Riffs of this subtune were used in the first Wackor EP in 1999 in the song 'Iced'." (NP) Highscore NecroPolo's own comments are denoted (NP).

SW1.4 + SW1.7 "This is the sibling of the other gameproject that I made for AVATAR because it had the very same workflow. I turned on my synth and started playing. I created a 3-channel session file in Reaper studio software with all the subtunes included then I converted the whole pack with Hermit's SWMconvert.exe, created instruments, adjusted sounds, packed exported files and so on. I wanted to use SIDwizard 1.7 because of its nice advanced functions but it turned out that it supports 6 subtunes only and I needed a couple more so I used the older SW1.4 for the ingame tunes instead because it can handle 16 subs. Only the title screen uses SW1.7. Despite the big number of subtunes, it was a really fast and fluent project." (NP) Main screen Ingame 01 Ingame 02 Ingame 03 Ingame 04 Ingame 05 Ingame 06 Ingame 07 Ingame 08 Main game screen tune NecroPolo's own comments are denoted (NP).

Globe prologue NecroPolo GT2.7 "SID was originally created for AGod (my API teammate) for his 3-screen pic. Because of some other releases that needed his pixel art the pic delayed so the tune was finally included in a SIDwave music collection. The original was composed for a show called 'The Globe' in 2008. The client picked a more guitar-oriented rock style intro so this short tune rested in the box for a while. 1:1 conversion." (NP) NecroPolo's own comments are denoted (NP).

GMC1.6 "That was my first complete track composed with Game Music Creator v1.6 and I stuck with its aggressive sound until the end of my early SID composer days. This tune was in the pack that was given for a demo group called "GMC" for their debut called "Brand New". I don't know if they used any of the songs later on but as I can remember they had some problems with the music driver. The original file had some bugs that were fixed by iAN CooG in 2009." (NP) NecroPolo's own comments are denoted (NP).
GMC2.0 - Original version of /MUSICIANS/N/NecroPolo/GP_Cars.sid, Subtunes 1 & 2, that had to be split on game author's request. NecroPolo's own comments are denoted (NP).

GMC1.6 + SW1.9-EMU "This game music pack has approximately a decade-old history. When we started to create stuff with LHS he mentioned that he has a race game project that was already 10 years old even by then. The very first music track I created for the game was a special edition of my engine FX tune Cadmium, around 2010. Then years passed, SID-Wizard and MIDI conversion came out. Many tiny tunes became added and detached from the project, like yellowstorm.sid that was intended to be used in GP Cars initially. Then the game started to get its final form in 2022, so did the music. The in-game tunes were created with the super-flexible SW-EMU. I must emphasize that the amazing 3...2...1... FX and most others are not mine. They were created by Hermit who is a much better sound designer than I've ever been." (NP) Intro Engine "V10 engine FX, created back in 1992 when Nigel Mansell became F1 champion. No, this is not a digi sound at all." (NP) Main Menu "Almost the same as Cadmium.sid just with a different ending and under the hood there is Wacek's GMC2.0 driver and not GMC1.6 that Cadmium has." (NP) Countdown "This speech FX is entirely created by Hermit. He also did the majority of ingame sound FX on channel3." (NP) Ingame 01 "All ingame tunes are 2-channel SIDs, converted from MIDI and assembled with SID-Wizard 1.9-EMU."
